Section 01

What Is a Network Interface?

A network interface is a physical port on a networking device that you can plug a cable into. It enables communication with other devices by accepting inbound traffic and forwarding outbound traffic — acting as transit between a source and a destination.

Two Categories of Traffic Processed

  • Transit traffic — flows through the device from a source to a destination (packets being routed between networks).
  • Exception traffic — traffic destined to the device itself, such as SSH management sessions, routing protocol messages (OSPF hellos, BGP updates), SNMP monitoring. Also called self-traffic. Covered in detail in the Junos OS Architecture: Control Plane and Data Plane module.
💡
Other Interface Types

Beyond physical network interfaces, Junos devices also have loopback, management, tunnel, virtual, service, and internal interfaces. This module covers network interfaces only.

🏷️
Section 02

Interface Naming Convention

Every network interface on a Junos device has a unique name encoding both interface type and physical location in the chassis:

Junos Interface Name Format
<type>-<FPC>/<PIC>/<Port>

Example:  xe-4/2/0

  xe = Interface type prefix  (10 Gigabit Ethernet)
   4 = FPC slot number        (line card slot 4)
   2 = PIC number             (section 2 of that line card)
   0 = Port number            (first port in that PIC section)

Note: ALL numbers start at zero.
Anatomy of a Junos interface name. Each segment encodes a specific piece of hardware location information. Numbering always starts at zero.
⚠️
Numbering Always Starts at Zero

The first FPC = 0, first PIC = 0, first port = 0. This is universal in computing and a common source of confusion for newcomers.

Why This Convention Matters

  • Universal across all Junos devices — same format on a 4-port fixed router and a 1000-port chassis. You always know how to read the name.
  • Unambiguous remote communication — when on a call with a remote engineer, both parties know exactly which physical port is being discussed.
  • Automation-friendly — one script can manage many different Junos devices without per-device port naming logic, because interface names always look the same regardless of device size or model.
📝
Occasional 3-Letter Prefixes

Some interface names begin with 3 or more letters. The 2-letter rule is correct for the vast majority of JNCIA-level devices.

⚡
Section 03

Interface Type Prefixes

Historically, many physical interface types existed (Serial, SONET/SDH, ATM). Today almost everything is Ethernet. The interface prefix reflects Ethernet speed.

PrefixFull NameSpeedNotes
feFast Ethernet100 MbpsLegacy — old devices only
geGigabit Ethernet1 GbpsCommon on many devices
xe10 Gigabit Ethernet10 GbpsX = Roman numeral for 10
etEthernet40 Gbps+Used when speed variety makes naming impractical
⚠️
Rare Exceptions

In rare cases, xe or et may differ due to underlying hardware. At JNCIA level, the definitions above are correct for the vast majority of devices.

Transceiver Terminology

  • SFP — Small Form-factor Pluggable
  • SFP+ — Enhanced SFP (typically 10 Gbps)
  • QSFP — Quad SFP (4× lanes; typically 40 Gbps+). The Q stands for Quad.
🔧
Section 04

FPC & PIC Hardware Terms

FPC — Flexible PIC Concentrator

  • The line card — larger removable card that slots into the chassis
  • Each FPC slot has a unique number printed on the chassis
  • Provides dedicated forwarding resources (bandwidth) to the PICs within it

PIC — Physical Interface Card

  • Strictly: smaller interface card that slots into an FPC for customization
  • Also used to describe one dedicated section of a line card with its own forwarding power
  • Appears as the middle number in interface names
🔍
Decoding xe-4/2/0 on an MX480

4 → FPC slot 4 (the line card in that chassis slot)

2 → PIC 2 (section 2 of that line card, or a physical sub-card)

0 → Port 0 (first port in PIC section 2)

Where These Terms Appear

  • Juniper documentation — specs like "X Gbps dedicated per PIC" in data sheets
  • Operational commands — show chassis fpc and show chassis pic display installed hardware (line cards, interface cards, individual SFP modules). These are advanced commands, not required at JNCIA level, but they use exactly these terms.
📦
Section 05

Fixed-Form Factor Devices

Fixed-form devices have ports built directly into the chassis with no removable line card slots. Junos uses the exact same naming convention on these devices.

MX204 Example (12-Port Fixed Chassis)

Behind the scenes, the MX204 has two PIC sections, each with dedicated bandwidth:

Port GroupTypeInterface NamesCount
Left groupQSFPxe-0/0/0 → xe-0/0/34 ports
Right groupSFP+xe-0/1/0 → xe-0/1/78 ports
✅
One Naming Convention for All Junos Devices

Whether a 4-port fixed router or a multi-slot chassis with hundreds of ports, all Junos interface names follow type-FPC/PIC/Port. You always immediately know how to read any interface name on any Junos device.

📏
Section 06

MTU: Layer 2 vs Layer 3

MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) is the largest size of packet or frame allowed into an interface. Any packet or frame exceeding the MTU is dropped.

There are two separate MTU values on a Junos interface — one on the physical interface and one on the logical unit:

Layer 2 MTU — Physical Interface

  • Contains: Ethernet header + IP header + Transport header + Payload
  • Default (no VLAN tag): 1,514 bytes
  • Default changes when VLAN tags are present (tags add overhead)

Layer 3 MTU — Logical Unit

  • Contains: IP header + Transport header + Payload
  • Default: 1,500 bytes
  • Does not include the Ethernet header
Layer 3 MTU (1500 bytes) vs Layer 2 MTU (1514 bytes, no VLAN tag). The 14-byte difference is the Ethernet header. Frames exceeding MTU are dropped.
📌
MTU in show interfaces Output

In show interfaces detail output, you will see 1,500 bytes on the logical unit and 1,514 bytes on the physical interface. Watch for these two numbers in upcoming labs.

💻
Section 07

The show interfaces Command

The primary tool for verifying interface status and configuration. Supports output modifiers that control verbosity:

CommandOutput VolumeKey Info Shown
show interfaces terse <ifname>Minimal (~6 lines)Admin/link status, IP addresses, protocol families
show interfaces brief <ifname>ConciseMore than terse, less than default
show interfaces <ifname>Standard (~25 lines)Full interface information
show interfaces detail <ifname>VerboseStatistical information, MTU, speed
show interfaces extensive <ifname>MaximumEverything including extended error counters
Junos CLI — Parameter Order Flexibility
# Both commands produce identical output:
show interfaces terse xe-0/1/1
show interfaces xe-0/1/1 terse

# Omit interface name to see ALL interfaces on the device:
show interfaces terse

# ALL includes: physical, logical, loopback, management,
# tunnel, service, virtual, internal, and more.
📝
Junos CLI is Hierarchical But Flexible

Junos OS is very hierarchical in CLI design, but generally allows flexibility in parameter ordering. Focus on learning the concept of commands rather than memorizing a rigid syntax order.

📋
Section 08

Reading show interfaces terse Output

Output for a single interface shows two rows: one for the physical interface and one for each logical unit:

CLI Output — show interfaces terse xe-0/1/1
Interface         Admin  Link  Proto  Local               Remote
xe-0/1/1          up     up
xe-0/1/1.0        up     up    inet   172.16.10.1/20
                                 inet6  2001:db8:0:10::1/64
                                        fe80::1/64

Column Definitions

ColumnMeaningValues
InterfaceWithout .N suffix = physical interface; with .0 (or .1, etc.) = logical unitxe-0/1/1 / xe-0/1/1.0
AdminWhether manually shut down via configurationup down
LinkWhether physical signal/connection is activeup down
ProtoLayer 3 protocol family on the unitinet (IPv4)  inet6 (IPv6)
LocalIP address configured on this unitIPv4 or IPv6 with prefix length

Junos Protocol Family Names

  • inet — Junos name for IPv4. Short for Internet, which derives from Internetwork (connecting networks together — the origin of the word "Internet").
  • inet6 — Junos name for IPv6.

IPv6 Address Entries

A unit with IPv6 configured shows two inet6 entries:

  • The explicitly configured global unicast address (e.g., 2001:db8:0:10::1/64)
  • An automatically generated link-local address starting with fe80:: — Junos generates this automatically; only used for communication on the local link; never routed.
📌
2001:db8::/32 — Documentation Range

The 2001:db8:: prefix is reserved exclusively for documentation, textbooks, and courses. You will see it frequently in all networking study material and RFCs.

🔀
Section 09

Physical Interface vs Logical Unit

Junos makes a strict, consistent distinction between physical settings and logical settings. Each belongs on a different level of the interface hierarchy.

One physical interface can host multiple logical units. Physical settings apply to the physical interface; logical/protocol settings apply independently to each unit.

Physical Interface (xe-0/1/1)

Hardware-layer properties

  • Interface speed
  • Duplex (full = send & receive simultaneously; half = one at a time)
  • Fiber or copper physical settings
  • Layer 2 MTU (default: 1,514 bytes)

Logical Unit (xe-0/1/1.0)

Protocol-layer properties

  • IPv4 address (family inet)
  • IPv6 address (family inet6)
  • Layer 3 MTU (default: 1,500 bytes)
  • VLAN tags (logical concept, not physical)

Key Rules About Logical Units

  • Junos documentation calls them logical units or simply units.
  • Other vendors call these sub-interfaces — same concept, different terminology.
  • With only one logical unit on a physical interface, it is always Unit 0 → interface name suffix .0 (e.g., xe-0/1/1.0).
  • One physical interface can host multiple logical units — this is how a single physical port serves multiple VLANs or subnets simultaneously.
🚀
Multiple Logical Units = Efficient Topology

Instead of three physical interfaces for three LAN subnets (wasteful), you can configure three logical units on one physical port — each unit with its own IP address and VLAN tag. This requires trunk port configuration (covered in the Junos OS Switches Part 2 module).

🟢
Section 10

Admin & Link Status

When an interface is fully operational, you see four "up" values in show interfaces terse output (Admin + Link for both the physical interface and its logical unit). Each has a distinct meaning:

The three key scenarios for Admin and Link status. Understanding the difference is a fundamental troubleshooting skill in Junos.

Admin Column

  • Whether the interface has been manually shut down via configuration (administratively disabled).
  • Interface in this state is called "admin down". In the terse output, shows as dn.
  • A classic troubleshooting technique: administratively disable and re-enable an interface ("bouncing" the port).

Link Column

  • Whether the physical signal is present (cable connected and valid signal on the wire).
  • Link status is always the same for both the physical interface and all its logical units — either both are up or both are down.

Physical vs Logical Admin Shutdown — Critical Distinction

⚠️
Shutting the Physical Interface Brings Down ALL Logical Units

If you administratively shut down the physical interface, every single logical unit on it also goes down, regardless of how many there are. All services using that physical port are affected.

✅
Selective Unit Shutdown Without Affecting Others

You can shut down a single logical unit while all other units on that physical interface remain up. In service-provider environments with 100 customers on one physical port, you can suspend exactly one customer's service (e.g., for non-payment) without disrupting any other customer.

🎯
Section 11

Junos Consistency Model

The physical/logical interface concept is not unique to Junos — almost every vendor uses it. However, some vendors apply it inconsistently, creating unnecessary complexity.

Vendor Inconsistency Example

Other Vendor CLI (Inconsistent)
# Case 1: IP address configured directly on physical interface
interface FastEthernet0/1
  ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0

# Case 2: Same vendor, but now with VLANs...
# IP must now go on logical sub-interfaces instead:
interface FastEthernet0/1.10
  encapsulation dot1q 10
  ip address 10.0.10.1 255.255.255.0

interface FastEthernet0/1.20
  encapsulation dot1q 20
  ip address 10.0.20.1 255.255.255.0

# The IP address location changes depending on whether VLANs are used!

Problems with This Inconsistency

  • Harder to learn — must remember multiple ways of doing the same thing.
  • Automation is more complex — scripts must check whether an IP address is on a physical or logical interface depending on context.

Junos Approach: Always Consistent

Junos Configuration (Always Consistent)
# Physical settings ALWAYS on the physical interface:
interfaces {
    xe-0/1/1 {
        description "Corporate LAN uplink";
        # Logical settings ALWAYS on a logical unit:
        unit 0 {
            family inet {
                address 172.16.10.1/20;
            }
            family inet6 {
                address 2001:db8:0:10::1/64;
            }
        }
    }
}
📌
Junos Golden Rule — No Exceptions

Junos always requires at least one logical unit on every physical interface. Physical settings go on the physical interface. Logical/protocol settings always go on the logical unit. No exceptions. No gotchas. One consistent system across every Junos device.

🧪
Section 12

Verification Lab: Reading LAN Interface Status

Scenario: verify three LAN interfaces on a customer router. Two tasks:

  1. Verify all LAN ports are up.
  2. Verify IP/subnet masks are correct per the network diagram.

Interface-to-LAN Assignment

InterfaceConnected ToExpected IPv4Expected IPv6
xe-0/1/1Corporate LAN172.16.10.1/202001:db8:0:10::1/64
xe-0/1/2Server LAN172.16.20.1/242001:db8:0:20::1/64
xe-0/1/3Guest LAN172.16.30.1/242001:db8:0:30::1/64

✓ xe-0/1/1 — Corporate LAN

CLI Output
show interfaces terse xe-0/1/1

Interface          Admin  Link  Proto  Local
xe-0/1/1           up     up
xe-0/1/1.0         up     up    inet   172.16.10.1/20    ✓ correct
                                 inet6  2001:db8:0:10::1/64  ✓ correct
                                        fe80::1/64  (auto link-local)
✅

Result: Interface up. Both IPv4 and IPv6 match the diagram. Both tasks passed.

⚠ xe-0/1/2 — Server LAN (IPv4 Error)

CLI Output
show interfaces terse xe-0/1/2

Interface          Admin  Link  Proto  Local
xe-0/1/2           up     up
xe-0/1/2.0         up     up    inet   172.16.200.1/24  ✗ should be 172.16.20.1/24
                                 inet6  2001:db8:0:20::1/64  ✓ correct
                                        fe80::2/64
⚠️

Error: IPv4 shows 172.16.200.1/24 — should be 172.16.20.1/24. Previous engineer typed 200 in the third octet instead of 20. IPv6 is correct. Interface is up. Requires configuration correction.

✗ xe-0/1/3 — Guest LAN (Two Errors)

CLI Output
show interfaces terse xe-0/1/3

Interface          Admin  Link  Proto  Local
xe-0/1/3           up     up
xe-0/1/3.0         up     up    inet   172.16.33.1/24   ✗ should be 172.16.30.1/24
                                 inet6  (no global address)          ✗ missing 2001:db8:0:30::1/64
                                        fe80::3/64  (only link-local present)
✗

Error 1: IPv4 shows 172.16.33.1/24 — should be 172.16.30.1/24. Third octet is 33 instead of 30.

Error 2: No IPv6 global unicast address configured — only the auto-generated link-local fe80:: address exists. Global address 2001:db8:0:30::1/64 is missing entirely.

Both errors require configuration correction. These will be fixed in the configuration module later in the course, along with hostname changes.

🔎
Section 13

Filtering Output & Interface Descriptions

Filtering show interfaces Output

Running show interfaces terse without a specified interface shows every interface on the device: physical, logical, loopback, management, tunnel, virtual, service, and internal. This output can be very long. You can narrow it:

Junos CLI — Filtering Examples
# All interfaces (includes internal/management/loopback/etc.):
show interfaces terse

# Specific named interface only:
show interfaces terse xe-0/1/1

# Wildcard: all interfaces whose name starts with "xe-0/1"
# (* matches any text after the specified prefix):
show interfaces terse xe-0/1*
# → Shows all 10GbE interfaces on PIC 1 of FPC 0
📌
Internal Interfaces at Top of Terse Output

When running unfiltered show interfaces terse, output begins with internal interfaces serving special purposes. These are normal — you do not need to worry about them at this stage. More powerful filtering options (pipe operators like | match, | find) are covered in Network Interfaces Part 2.

show interfaces description

Junos lets you add a text description to any interface or logical unit. The command shows all configured descriptions compactly:

CLI Output — show interfaces description
show interfaces description

Interface     Admin  Link  Description
xe-0/1/1      up     up    Corporate LAN uplink
xe-0/1/2      up     up    Server Farm connection
xe-0/1/3      up     up    Guest WiFi SSID
💡
First Command on a New Device

Many experienced engineers run show interfaces description as one of the first commands when logging on to an unfamiliar device. With a well-maintained description standard, this gives an immediate high-level view of every interface's purpose — "the lay of the land." Descriptions can be applied to both physical interfaces and individual logical units.

Section 14

Command Quick Reference

show interfaces terseShow ALL interfaces — physical, logical, internal, management, loopback, tunnel, service, virtual
show interfaces terse <ifname>Show terse output for one specific interface and its logical units
show interfaces <ifname> terseIdentical to above — parameter order is flexible
show interfaces terse xe-0/1*Wildcard filter: show only interfaces starting with "xe-0/1"
show interfaces brief <ifname>Brief output: more than terse, less than default
show interfaces <ifname>Default output (~25 lines): full interface information
show interfaces detail <ifname>Verbose: statistical info, speed, MTU
show interfaces extensive <ifname>Maximum output: everything including extended error counters
show interfaces descriptionAll interfaces with admin/link status and their configured descriptions
show chassis fpcShow installed FPC (line card) hardware — advanced command
show chassis picShow installed PIC (interface card/section) hardware — advanced command

Key Terms Reference

TermDefinition
FPCFlexible PIC Concentrator — the line card that slots into a chassis
PICPhysical Interface Card — sub-card that slots into an FPC, or a dedicated forwarding section of an FPC
SFPSmall Form-factor Pluggable transceiver module
SFP+Enhanced SFP; typically 10 Gbps
QSFPQuad SFP — 4-lane transceiver; typically 40 Gbps+. Q = Quad.
MTUMaximum Transmission Unit — largest packet/frame allowed into an interface; oversized frames are dropped
Layer 2 MTUFull frame size including Ethernet header (default: 1,514 bytes, no VLAN tag)
Layer 3 MTUIP packet size, no Ethernet header (default: 1,500 bytes)
Logical unitJunos term for a sub-interface / logical interface on a physical interface
Unit 0The default first logical unit; interface name shows as ifname.0
inetJunos protocol family name for IPv4 (short for Internetwork)
inet6Junos protocol family name for IPv6
Admin downInterface manually disabled via configuration; shows dn in Admin column
Link downPhysical signal not present; always same state for physical interface and all its logical units
Transit trafficTraffic flowing through the device between two external endpoints
Exception trafficTraffic destined to or originating from the device itself (SSH, routing protocols, monitoring)
V4 / V6Engineer shorthand for IPv4 / IPv6
Link-local (fe80::)Auto-generated IPv6 address; only valid on local link; never routed; generated automatically by Junos
2001:db8::/32IPv6 documentation range; reserved for use in textbooks, courses, and RFCs
